planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in fall in well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky upland soil; this dry-bluff species resents heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: A little-known small tree of dry bluffs, ridgetops, and upland pine-oak woods across the Alabama-Georgia-Florida panhandle corridor, closely related to black cherry but shorter-statured with smoother, more reddish young bark and a tidier crown. Short racemes of white flowers open in early spring before full leaf-out, followed by small black cherries relished by songbirds in summer. Best suited to a dry, sunny to lightly shaded slope where it will not compete with moisture-loving species, and useful where a native cherry is wanted on thin, well-drained soils unsuited to Prunus serotina. Rarely offered in the trade but worth seeking out from regional native-plant nurseries for woodland-edge restoration.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into deep, excessively drained white or yellow sand with full sun exposure; this species is restricted to ancient scrub dunes and will not tolerate shade or moisture retention.

directions: A federally endangered shrub found only on the ancient inland sand ridges of central Florida, notably the Lake Wales Ridge, where it forms low, crooked-branched thickets by root sprouting in the open gaps between scrub oaks and sand pines. Small white flowers appear on bare, zigzagging twigs in late winter, well before the narrow leaves emerge, followed by small yellow-green to reddish plums that feed scrub jays and other wildlife. Because its entire range is threatened by development, plants grown from nursery-propagated, documented-origin stock are valuable for ex-situ conservation plantings and scrub-habitat restoration gardens. Give it the driest, sandiest, most nutrient-poor spot available and resist the urge to irrigate or fertilize once established.

planting.note: Set out container-grown trees in warm weather well after all frost danger, in a sheltered hammock-like setting; this tropical species is damaged or killed by hard freezes.

directions: An evergreen hammock tree of extreme south Florida and the wider Caribbean, with glossy, laurel-like leaves that give it a refined, almost ornamental look distinct from the deciduous temperate cherries. Slender spikes of small white flowers appear intermittently through the warm months, followed by small dark cherries that draw a steady stream of mockingbirds, catbirds, and other fruit-eating birds. In cultivation it makes a dense, shapely screen, hedge, or specimen tree for hammock restoration and wildlife gardens in Miami-Dade, the Keys, and similarly frost-free pockets of the coast. It tolerates both full sun and the dappled light of an established hammock canopy but needs protection from any freezing weather.
